gptr can keep the code an agent executed beside the prompt that requested it. In a designated
R script, the code goes below the owning `peter()` statement between marker comments; in a
report or notebook, it becomes a chunk or cell. A fresh recorded block can run again as R
without another model request. Replaying still executes its R code, with the effects and
input dependencies that code has.

The executed examples use fake providers and separate work environments. Recording and
file-writing recipes are shown as code to run deliberately in your own temporary project.

## Calls in ordinary R scripts and functions

`peter()` is an R function. A helper can call it, inspect the returned session, and pass its
answer to other R code. Give it an environment when results should outlive the helper call.


``` r
library(gptr)
work = new.env()
work$mtcars = mtcars
fake = gptr_fake_provider(list(
  list(tool = "r", input = list(code = "top = head(mtcars[order(-mtcars$mpg), c('mpg', 'wt')], 3)")),
  "The three most fuel-efficient cars are stored in top."
))

rank_cars = function(data, model, envir) {
  peter("Find the three most fuel-efficient cars.", data = force(data), model = model, envir = envir,
        mode = auto)
}
s = rank_cars(work$mtcars, fake, work)
s$text
#> [1] "The three most fuel-efficient cars are stored in top."
work$top
#>                 mpg    wt
#> Toyota Corolla 33.9 1.835
#> Fiat 128       32.4 2.200
#> Honda Civic    30.4 1.615
summary(s)
#>  turn        role                                               preview tools
#>     1        user              Find the three most fuel-efficient cars.
#>     1   assistant                                                           r
#>     1 tool_result                              + top <data.frame 3 x 2>     r
#>     1   assistant The three most fuel-efficient cars are stored in top.
#>  tokens
#>      10
#>    1636
#>       6
#>    1639
```

The named `data = force(data)` supplies the helper's argument as an explicit context value:
its formal `data` is not a binding in `work`. If you attach an object by name instead, it must
be visible from the environment where the session evaluates.

`summary(s)` reads a compact table of recorded turns without a model call; it does not
produce a narrative or an executable workflow.

This works in an R file, but a call nested inside a function, loop or another expression does
not own a document block. It may run another model request when the script is executed
again. Keep calls whose agent code you want recorded as top-level statements; keep reusable
ordinary R calculations in functions. System 1 cache hits have their own rules and do not
make an arbitrary loop into a recorded workflow.

## Continuing one session with a pipe


``` r
follow = gptr_fake_provider(list("A first answer.", "An answer incorporating the follow-up."),
                            name = "follow")
first = peter("Summarize the analysis.", model = follow, envir = new.env())
second = first |> peter("Mention the sample size too.")
identical(first, second)
#> [1] TRUE
second$turns
#> [1] 2
```

A pipe adds turns to the same mutable session. A top-level pipe chain is one statement for
recording; its executed code follows that chain. `gptr_fork()` explicitly branches a session;
assigning it to another variable does not branch it.

## Recording a designated R script

`gptr_doc(path)` binds a document and supplies explicit consent to write blocks into it.
`gptr_doc()` reports the binding; `gptr_doc(FALSE)` removes it. It does not create a workflow
from past conversation turns.

For an offline recording exercise, save this as `analysis.R` in a temporary directory:


``` r
library(gptr)
fake = gptr_fake_provider(list(
  list(tool = "r", input = list(
    code = "top = head(mtcars[order(-mtcars$mpg), c('mpg', 'wt')], 3)",
    note = "ranked by mpg; ties keep the order of the data")),
  "The selected rows are in top."
))
result = peter("Find the three most fuel-efficient cars.", model = fake, mode = auto)
top
```

Then run it from a separate driver or at the console:


``` r
gptr_doc("analysis.R")
work = new.env()
gptr_source("analysis.R", replay = "auto", envir = work)
gptr_blocks("analysis.R")
gptr_doc(FALSE)
```

The missing block causes a fake model request, and the executed code is recorded below the
call. The header identifies the block, model, date and prompt hash; the body hash identifies
its recorded code. `## Decision:` retains a model-supplied note, and `#>` retains bounded
output. A note is a model explanation, not proof that the code is correct.

The document must be writable, and recording needs consent. `gptr_doc(path)` supplies that
consent explicitly; `record = "off"` prevents automatic recording into discovered documents.
To opt out for one call, including a call in a bound document, pass
`.opts = list(record = FALSE)`. Pass it to each call in a pipe chain that should not record.
`record = TRUE` in `.opts` keeps the usual consent checks; it does not supply consent.
Without a binding, source discovery can find a call in a document. At an interactive console,
agreeing to transcript recording creates a script under `.gptr/transcripts/`; an explicit
`gptr_doc(path, format = "transcript")` selects an R transcript target.

Main-session recorded code runs as ordinary document code on replay. Keep its input objects
in the document's evaluation environment, using `peter()`'s default caller environment. An
arbitrary custom `envir` is not restored or applied to the following recorded chunk. For a
function that works in a separate environment, opt out with `.opts = list(record = FALSE)`
and keep its executable steps explicitly in the function. Forks and team children have their
own recorded overlay wrappers.

## Inspecting and replaying


``` r
gptr_doc("analysis.R")
listing = gptr_blocks("analysis.R")
listing[, c("id", "status", "model", "date", "tokens", "cost")]

gptr_source("analysis.R", replay = "replay", envir = new.env())
gptr_cache()
gptr_doc(FALSE)
```

`gptr_source()` executes **`.R` files only**, expression by expression. It can regenerate a
stale block and skip its old code in the same run, which base `source()` cannot do. Its return
value is a block listing with the action taken for each block. `gptr_blocks()` reads R,
R Markdown, Quarto and Jupyter formats; pending writes can be recovered before listing.

| Replay mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `"auto"` | Replay fresh blocks; run missing or stale calls through the selected model. |
| `"replay"` | Never call a model; a missing or stale record signals `gptr_error_not_recorded`. |
| `"live"` | Ask the model again and rewrite recorded blocks when writing is allowed. |
| `"record"` | Regenerate stale blocks; fresh blocks replay. |

A call's `replay =` argument wins over process options, the `GPTR_REPLAY` environment variable
and settings. For a script intended to run without model calls:

```sh
GPTR_REPLAY=replay Rscript --vanilla analysis.R
```

This checks that the requested calls can use their records; it does not certify the analysis,
freeze package versions, capture external datasets or make file/network operations in the
recorded R code safe to repeat. Verify data paths, dependencies, outputs and side effects.

`gptr_blocks()` marks a block `fresh`, `stale`, `user-edited` or `undone`. Changed prompts or
interpolated values can invalidate replay; the listing alone cannot evaluate runtime
interpolation. Hand-edited code is recognized by its changed hash. Undone code stays visible
as inert comments. Keep the associated answer cache if the replayed calls need their text or
values; the code block and the cache are different parts of the record.

`gptr_cache()` reports System 1 and System 2 answer caches, temporary spill files and pending
sidecars. `gptr_cache("prune")` removes entries no longer in use or beyond their retention
window; `gptr_cache("clear", "s2")` removes System 2 answers. Clearing answers can change what
is available during replay. Pending document sidecars are not deleted by cache cleanup;
apply them with `gptr_doc(path, sync = TRUE)`.

## R Markdown, Quarto and Jupyter

In `.Rmd` and `.qmd`, a recorded block becomes a chunk labeled `gptr-<id>` after its calling
chunk. Bind the report, run it with its normal renderer, then inspect the recorded blocks:


``` r
gptr_doc("analysis.Rmd")
rmarkdown::render("analysis.Rmd")
gptr_blocks("analysis.Rmd")
gptr_doc(FALSE)
```

Use Quarto's renderer for `.qmd`; `gptr_source()` is not a renderer for either format. Arrange
the document's setup to load gptr, prepare its input data and select a model or replay mode.
Plain R chunks still execute when the report is rendered.

For Jupyter, bind the saved `.ipynb` path in the R kernel. Blocks become agent cells. Writes
are queued while the notebook is open to avoid competing with the notebook editor; after
closing it, apply the pending blocks:


``` r
gptr_doc("analysis.ipynb")
# Run the notebook's Peter calls in its R kernel, then save and close the notebook.
gptr_doc("analysis.ipynb", sync = TRUE)
gptr_blocks("analysis.ipynb")
gptr_doc(FALSE)
```

A notebook edited since a pending block was queued may need conflict resolution. Reopening
or listing a file is not proof that pending blocks were applied successfully.

## Asking Peter to summarize a completed workflow

Choose the deliverable explicitly. A history document, an ordinary executable script and a
narrative summary have different roles. gptr provides recording and replay APIs; it has no
one-call export that guarantees an arbitrary conversation becomes a complete executable
workflow.

With your own live-model session `s`, ask for a narrative by making a model request such as:


``` r
summary_session = s |> peter(
  "Summarize the steps actually completed, decisions, inputs, outputs and unresolved issues.\nKeep proposed work separate from completed work; name saved files only if verified.",
  mode = plan
)
summary_session$text
```

The answer is **model-generated text** and adds a turn to `s`. Check its claims against the
workspace, files and history before treating it as a record. `gptr_usage(s)` shows the
request's usage; a summary request is not free merely because it summarizes existing work.

For a Peter history document, designate the target before recording top-level prompts,
include ordinary R setup and checks, and inspect the blocks and replay behavior. To assemble
one from earlier work, ask the model to draft it and review the draft; earlier unrecorded
turns are not automatically recovered into validated blocks.

For an ordinary R script, request a separate, explicit implementation:


``` r
script_session = s |> peter(
  "Draft an ordinary R script implementing the verified analysis.\nInclude libraries, input paths, parameters, computations and explicit output saves.\nDo not call Peter; identify any missing input or step instead of inventing it.",
  mode = plan
)
script_session$text
```

This returns **model-generated output**, not an exported or validated script. Save only
reviewed code, then run it in a fresh environment with the intended inputs and verify its
outputs. A prose summary can accompany either script, but prose alone is not executable
history.

See `vignette("system-one", package = "gptr")` for typed decisions and
`vignette("teams-and-background", package = "gptr")` for orchestration and SDK control.
